core.title: Do not let a test disable itself; exclude it at the runner level instead
core.given: A test case exists in a test suite.
core.when: the test is disabled from inside its own source — a skip-, todo- or expected-failure-style modifier, or an early return guarded on an environment check
core.then: Remove the self-disabling so the test actually runs (or delete the test); if it must not run somewhere, exclude it in the runner's configuration instead.
prefer: Remove the modifier and let the test run, or delete the test.
Exclude via a runner config filter: visible in configuration, not invisible in a green suite.
avoid: A skip- or todo-style modifier on a test case.
An early return guarded on an environment value inside a test body: same fault in disguise, more common, silent exactly where nobody watches.
An expected-failure marker used as a disabler. Unresolved source conflict: one clause forbids it, another treats expected-failure markers as accepted RED-phase markers. Escalate, don't decide.
unless: Skip in a fixture/helper that is not itself a test case.
Runner-level exclusion (config filter), the supported way not to run a test.
core.why: A skipped test reports GREEN: the suite passes, the gate sees no failure, and the acceptance is recorded as covered by a test that did not run.
evidence: The convention check reports no finding of a self-disabled test or a guarded early return for the test files in scope.
Any environment-specific non-execution is expressed as a runner configuration filter visible in config, not inside the test body.
verification: Strict disposition: the check fails on every finding; it has no advisory mode and no ratchet baseline. Severity 3.
Scope: only test cases. Self-disabling constructs inside fixtures or helpers that are not themselves test cases are out of scope, and runner-level configuration exclusions are not findings.

The check detects, structurally, self-disabling modifiers on test cases and environment-guarded early returns inside test bodies; a stack realization detects its own constructs for its own test-framework idioms. Stack scope and any changed-file filtering are implementation scope of the check, not limits on the obligation, which applies to any test case in any test file, whatever the language or test framework, changed or not, whether or not the file carries an assigned test-role.

An expected-failure marker used as a disabler is an unresolved source conflict (one clause forbids it, another accepts such markers as RED-phase markers): the check must surface those cases for authoritative resolution rather than silently pass or fail them.

fires: A test case carries a skip-style modifier (the test is marked skipped).
A test case is marked todo / not-yet-implemented.
An expected-failure marker is used as a disabler.
A live test (for example a smoke test) begins with an early return guarded on an environment value, so it silently passes when the value is absent.
An existing, unchanged test file already contains a self-disabling construct or a guarded early return.
doesNotFire: A skip-style construct or guarded early return inside a fixture or helper that is not itself a test case.
A test excluded from a run via the runner's configuration filter.

profileRequirements.meaning: Which test runner the stack uses, and therefore whose run configuration is the visible place to exclude a test that must not run in some environment (the remedy the core prescribes instead of in-body self-disabling).

neutralityNotes: The obligation itself is stack-neutral and the core carries it in full, including the unresolved expected-failure-marker conflict (escalate, don't decide) and the strict disposition. Round-2 corrections: (1) core.when now prohibits early returns guarded on an environment check only — bun.json never extends the guarded-return prohibition to arbitrary configuration checks, so no broader reading is added; (2) activation keeps the source's generic file-kind scope ('test' = any test case in any test file) instead of enumerating the roles unit_test/acceptance_test/e2e_test, because bun.json supplies no role assignment that guarantees every test file receives one of those roles — an enumerated-role predicate would let unassigned or other test files escape the obligation; core:verification states explicitly that the obligation is not limited by language, test framework, changed-file filtering or role assignment, and given likewise carries no role enumeration. What could not be made neutral, and stayed in the Bun realization: the literal test-framework modifier names (`.skip`, `.todo`, `.failing`, `.fails`), the `it`/`test`/`describe` call forms, the `process.env` environment-guard syntax, and this rule's detector/term/finding ids (bun_tester_discipline_detector, self_skip, guarded_bail) — the core's verification names the check generically, per the notProfileKeys policy. The activation fires/doesNotFire examples were neutralized the same way; their concrete Bun literals are preserved in bun.json itself, which is delivered as the reference example. Which files count as test files is treated as detection scope of the check (implementation scope, per the source itself), and bun.json states no suffix or path values, so no suffix/roles profile key is required. The only profile datum the core needs is the stack's test runner (tooling.test_runner, an existing key), which names where the visible configuration-level exclusion lives; no new vocabulary key was necessary.
